query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is controlled by the selective oxidation of the minor alloying element X (where X is Si, Mn, or Al), which promotes the in‐situ formation of an oxide that is compositionally and structurally compatible with the substrate. This compatibility minimizes thermal expansion mismatch and internal stress, thus preventing oxide cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: High temperature (≥900 °C) and a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment for prolonged durations
generation.structural_mediator: A slow-growing, coherent oxide scale enriched in the oxidized X element that forms a well-adhered, low-stress interlayer at the metal/oxide interface
generation.mechanism: The minor X element (Si, Mn, or Al) preferentially oxidizes at high temperature, creating an oxide layer whose crystallographic structure and thermal expansion closely match that of the underlying alloy. This selective oxidation slows further oxygen ingress and limits stress accumulation, thereby suppressing the formation of cracks and spallation of the oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: An adherent, coherent oxide layer that grows slowly over time, maintaining a low defect density and resisting thermal stresses that would otherwise cause cracking or spallation, unlike compositions without sufficient X enrichment or with accelerated oxide growth kinetics.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloys or variants with insufficient reactive X element addition that develop either unstable, rapidly growing oxide layers or scales prone to cracking/spallation under similar high-temperature oxidative exposures
generation.boundary: Behavior is expected at service temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments; deviations may occur at significantly lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing conditions
generation.uncertainty: The exact influence of each specific X element (Si, Mn, or Al) on oxide adherence and growth kinetics, and the interplay between multiphase microstructures and oxide scale formation, require further quantification

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with variations in the X element (using Si, Mn, and Al) and a control alloy lacking the reactive X element. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for an extended period (e.g., 200 hours). Characterize the oxide layers using microscopy (TEM/SEM), X-ray diffraction (for phase identification), and adhesion testing (e.g., pull-off tests) to assess oxide coherence, thickness, and spallation behavior.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness versus time using cross-sectional TEM/SEM
Crystallographic phase and composition analysis of the oxide scale (via XRD and XPS)
Interfacial adhesion strength (via standardized adhesion tests)
Residual stress measurements in the oxide layer (using X-ray stress analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the selective oxidation of the X element is not controlling the oxide stability, then (a) the samples with different X elements will not exhibit significantly more coherent, slow-growing, and adherent oxide layers than the control alloy, or (b) all samples will show similar oxide cracking or spallation behavior irrespective of the X element addition.

Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior of Dual-Phase High Entropy Alloy for Concentrating Solar Power Systems

Abstract: Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205.
